items.title: Nurse academics' experiences and perceptions of artificial intelligence in education, research, clinical practice and nursing management: a qualitative descriptive study
items.abstract: Background Nurse academics educate future nurses and nurse managers and often hold managerial roles, yet existing research has examined artificial intelligence (AI) in education, research, clinical practice and nursing management separately and mostly through surveys. This study aimed to explore nurse academics' experiences, perceptions and expectations regarding AI across academic work, nursing education, clinical practice and nursing management. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with 17 nurse academics in Türkiye selected by criterion sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed in MAXQDA using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Coded segments were descriptively quantitized and code saturation was assessed. The study is reported according to the COREQ checklist. Results Nine themes and 47 codes (405 coded segments) were identified. Participants positioned AI as an assistant rather than a replacement for the nurse. AI was used most intensively in academic work, whereas clinical experience remained limited. In nursing management, use for duty rostering, in-service training planning and documentation stood out, and AI-generated rosters were reported to strengthen perceived fairness among nurses. Reliability, ethical and security concerns formed the most extensive theme, and verifying AI outputs against sources was the most frequently coded strategy. Although almost all participants used AI, 14 did not feel ready or competent and requested structured training. Participants emphasised that the final decision must remain with the nurse; most showed opportunity-oriented but conditional adoption. Conclusions Nurse academics adopt AI as a supportive tool under human oversight. Perceived lack of competence and concerns about the reliability of information are the main barriers to adoption. Nursing schools and healthcare organisations should provide structured AI literacy training, develop guidelines on output verification and data protection, and transparently pilot AI-assisted rostering in which the final decision remains with the nurse manager.

items.title: Nursing Undergraduate Teachers’ Cognition Of AI-Driven Teacher-Student Education al Co-Creation: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping nursing education, and AI‑driven teacher‑student co‑creation has emerged as a promising approach to cultivate human‑AI collaboration competencies. Teachers, as designers and facilitators, play a pivotal role; their cognition, attitudes, and practices determine the effectiveness of co‑creation. Ethical Dimension: This study was performed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhengzhou University (No. ZZUIRB2025‑56). Methods From January to February 2026, 232 teachers from nursing colleges in Henan Province, China, were recruited via convenience sampling. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire, a self‑developed Cognition of AI‑Driven Teacher‑Student Educational Co‑Creation Questionnaire, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale(AILS), and the Flourishing Scale(FS). Descriptive statistics, t‑tests, ANOVA, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression were used. Results The mean total cognition score was 116.38(SD = 13.90). Cognition positively correlated with flourishing (r = 0.380, p < 0.01) and AI literacy (r = 0.402, p < 0.01). AI literacy (β = 0.285) and flourishing (β = 0.241) were independent positive factors. The model explained 21.6% of the variance (adjusted R 2 = 0.205, F = 6.947). Conclusion Nursing undergraduate teachers showed favourable overall cognition, yet cognitive understanding and practical engagement lagged behind attitudes. AI literacy and flourishing are key modifiable associated factors. Multifaceted interventions—structured AI literacy training, psychological resource cultivation, and institutional support—are needed to strengthen cognitive foundations and bridge the gap between positive attitudes and sustained co‑creation practices in nursing education.

items.title: Occupational Burnout and Psychological Well-Being Among Journalists in Spain and Germany
items.abstract: Background: Journalism is a high-demand occupation characterised by sustained time pressure, emotional demands, and exposure to potentially distressing events, making occupational burnout and psychological well-being important concerns. This study examined psychological and occupational well-being and burnout-related indicators among journalists in Spain and Germany, focusing on country and gender differences. Methods: This study employed a cross-sectional design. The participants comprised 227 professional journalists (Spain: n = 115; Germany: n = 112; 108 men and 119 women) recruited via non-probability convenience sampling. Workplace well-being, global life satisfaction, happiness, professional quality of life, and burnout were assessed using standardised questionnaires. Descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlations, and independent-sample t-tests were performed. Welch’s correction was used when required and Holm’s procedure was applied to families with multiple comparisons. Effect sizes were expressed as Cohen’s d with 95% confidence intervals. Results: The mean Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) total score was 15.61 (standard deviation [SD] = 2.76), while mean scores were 31.22 (SD = 6.30) for compassion satisfaction, 24.75 (SD = 6.20) for Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) burnout and 20.94 (SD = 13.43) for Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) emotional exhaustion. Workplace resources were positively associated with happiness in the current position (r = 0.57 to 0.74, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). ProQOL burnout and emotional exhaustion were negatively associated with well-being indicators (r = –0.62 to –0.29, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). No statistically significant country differences were identified and the effect sizes were negligible or small. After Holm’s adjustment, women reported higher compassion satisfaction (mean [M] = 33.30, SD = 5.50 vs. M = 28.92, SD = 6.36; d = –0.74), ProQOL burnout (M = 26.59, SD = 5.86 vs. M = 22.67, SD = 6.02; d = –0.66) and emotional exhaustion (M = 24.52, SD = 13.84 vs. M = 16.92, SD = 11.97; d = –0.59). Conclusions: In this non-probability sample, positive occupational and psychological indicators coexisted with burnout-related strain. The results indicate associations rather than causal effects, and highlight the need for further longitudinal and country-adjusted research on journalists’ occupational health.

items.title: Occupational Health Hazards and Safety Protocol Compliance among Clinical Staff across Tertiary and Secondary Healthcare Facilities in Gombe State, Nigeria: A Multi-Center Cross-Sectional Analysis
items.abstract: Background Healthcare practitioners routinely confront diverse biological, physical, ergonomic, chemical, and psychological hazards. Sustained adherence to Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) guidelines and personal protective equipment (PPE) protocols remains central to preventing occupational injuries, controlling nosocomial infections, and safeguarding workforce capacity. However, baseline empirical data regarding safety compliance and hazard distribution across different health facility tiers in North-Eastern Nigeria are limited. Objective This study evaluated occupational safety practices, institutional safety policy awareness, and hazard exposure patterns among clinical personnel across five major public healthcare facilities in Gombe State. Methods We conducted a multi-center cross-sectional quantitative survey across seven clinical professions (Nursing/Midwifery, Medicine, Medical Laboratory Science, Pharmacy, Physiotherapy, Radiography, and Dentistry). A multi-stage stratified proportionate random sampling framework was applied to a regional clinical workforce of N pop = 1,450 across five hospitals (Federal Teaching Hospital Gombe, State Specialist Hospital Gombe, Federal Medical Centre Kumo, General Hospital Bajoga, and General Hospital Kaltungo). To achieve adequate statistical power and preserve an Events Per Variable ratio > 25 for multivariable modeling, 575 questionnaires were distributed. We retrieved n = 502 valid questionnaires (87.3% response rate; covering 34.6% of the regional clinical workforce). Data were gathered using a validated tool adapted from the Weymouth Portland Health and Safety Self-Assessment Questionnaire (α = 0.83, Content Validity Index = 0.88). Chi-square tests (ꭓ 2), Cramér’s V effect sizes, and multivariable binary logistic regression models (reporting Adjusted Odds Ratios [aOR] and 95% Confidence Intervals [95% CI]) were performed (p < 0.05). Results Ergonomic strain emerged as the dominant hazard, with 76.5% (n = 384) of participants experiencing work-related musculoskeletal disorders primarily low back pain (51.2%) and neck/shoulder discomfort (25.3%) followed by high workload-related psychological stress (69.7%). Biological exposures were frequent: 56.4% reported mucosal or skin contact with blood and body fluids, while 43.2% sustained percutaneous needle-stick or sharps injuries within the preceding 12 months. PPE adherence varied widely: standard glove utilization was high (93.2%), whereas use of facial protection (68.1%), protective gowns (47.4%), specialized safety footwear (31.5%), and protective eyewear or face shields (23.1%) was limited. Supply chain deficits and institutional stock-outs were identified by 80.5% of respondents as the primary obstacle to compliance, with secondary state hospitals reporting significantly higher stock-out frequencies than the federal tertiary center (p < 0.001). Hazard patterns differed significantly across professions (ꭓ 2 = 82.45, df = 6, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.30). Multivariable logistic regression revealed that ≥ 5 years of clinical experience (aOR = 2.68, 95% CI: 1.82–3.95, p < 0.001) and completion of formal institutional OSH orientation (aOR = 3.42, 95% CI: 2.28–5.13, p < 0.001) independently predicted high PPE compliance. Conversely, nurses and physicians faced greater odds of percutaneous injury compared to allied health controls (aOR = 3.38, 95% CI: 2.21–5.17, p < 0.001). Conclusion Healthcare workers across public tertiary and secondary facilities in Gombe State experience notable ergonomic strain, psychological stress, and biological exposures. Although basic barrier practices are common, widespread compliance with comprehensive PPE protocols is hampered by supply deficits especially within secondary general hospitals and incomplete safety onboarding for early-career staff. Institutional safety management, mandatory orientation programs, ergonomic workspace adjustments, and stable supply procurement are needed to protect clinical personnel. items.title: PatternMiner: Automated Mathematical Discovery Through LLM-Guided Training and Interpretation of Small Models
items.abstract: There are several approaches to AI-driven mathematical discovery. One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.

items.title: Pedagogical Aspects of AI in Tourism Education: A Comparative Analysis of Empirical Studies
items.abstract: This study explores the pedagogical aspects of artificial intelligence (AI) application in tourism education. It presents a comparative analysis of empirical studies focusing on the integration of AI technologies into the educational process in higher education institutions. The research examines the opportunities and challenges of using AI in tourism education, with particular attention to teaching methods, personalized learning, student engagement, digital competencies, and the development of professional skills. The study aims to identify current trends in AI-supported education and evaluate its potential contribution to improving the quality of tourism education. The findings highlight the importance of integrating innovative digital technologies into educational practices to prepare future tourism professionals for the changing demands of the tourism industry.

items.title: Perceived Quality of Siloed versus Time-Synchronized Data Architectures for AI-Based Digital Mental Health: A Within-Subjects Scenario Study
items.abstract: Fragmented data architectures may limit how artificial intelligence (AI)-based digital mental health systems combine and communicate multimodal information. This scenario-based study tested whether users perceived the Integrated framework more favorably than the Traditional framework. U.S. adults familiar with digital mental health technologies reviewed standardized descriptions of both conditions and rated system quality, information quality, and perceived transparency and explainability. The constructs covered data quality, portability, response time, accuracy, timeliness, completeness, transparency, and explainability. Paired-samples t tests were supplemented by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Valid paired samples were 277, 267, and 258 for the three constructs, respectively. Ratings favored the Integrated condition for system quality (M = 3.47 vs. 3.38; t (276) = −2.66, P = 0.008, |dz| = 0.16), information quality (M = 3.48 vs. 3.34; t (266) = −4.49, P dz| = 0.28), and perceived transparency and explainability (M = 3.79 vs. 3.65; t (257) = −3.04, P = 0.003, |dz| = 0.19). Nonparametric analyses supported the same conclusions. Absolute paired effect magnitudes ranged from |dz| = 0.16 to |dz| = 0.28. Because participants evaluated descriptions rather than functioning systems and temporal alignment was bundled with integration, the findings identify a modest perceptual advantage rather than causal, technical, or clinical-performance benefits. The results support further user-centered prototype and implementation testing.

items.title: Perceptions and Challenges of Integrating Artificial Intelligence in English Teaching in Iraqi Secondary Schools: A Comparative Study of Private and Public Sector
items.abstract: This study compares the private and public education sectors using a quantitative survey approach to examine the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English teaching among 189 secondary school teachers in Iraq. Significant sector differences are revealed by the results, which show that private school teachers were more aware of AI, had better facilities, and used it more in the classroom. Inadequate teacher training (84.1%), deficiencies in tech infrastructure (78.3%), financial limitations (71.4%), a lack of institutional support (69.3%), and teacher opposition to change (63.0%) are the main obstacles to implementation. However, educators in both fields demonstrated favorable opinions regarding AI, acknowledging its benefits for improving student engagement, personalizing instruction, giving instant feedback, and fostering the development of 21st-century abilities. The study recommends infrastructure improvement, equal resource distribution to public schools, structured teacher training, and supportive rules and regulations to enable successful AI application.

items.title: Perceptions of the Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Radiology Workflow and Professional Roles: A Cross-Sectional Study at King Abdulaziz Medical City, Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now entering radiology, where they can analyze imaging data quantitatively and lessen dependence on subjective visual reading. This study investigated the perceived impact of AI implementation on radiology workflows and the professional roles of radiologists in the radiology department at King Abdulaziz Medical City (KAMC), Saudi Arabia. Methods: This study used a cross-sectional design at KAMC in Saudi Arabia. An online questionnaire was distributed to radiologists working at KAMC locations in Jeddah, Riyadh, and Al-Ahsa. A total of 100 participants responded. Demographic data, including gender, age, department, and professional rank, were collected and analyzed in Microsoft Excel and R version 4.2.2 (31 October 2022; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) in RStudio version 2026.01.1+403 (Posit PBC, Boston, MA, USA). Results: 81% of participants agreed or strongly agreed that AI would reduce time and improve healthcare, and 82% that it could improve image interpretation and reduce false-positive and false-negative errors. In addition, 69% agreed or strongly agreed that AI may reduce radiologists’ workload, and 56% that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages. However, 38% agreed that AI may reduce radiologists’ job opportunities, 33% were concerned about possible loss of patient data, and only 43% would trust AI to make an accurate diagnosis. No significant differences were found by gender or professional rank; across departments, only the perception that AI’s advantages outweigh its disadvantages differed significantly (p = 0.004), with interventional radiologists agreeing less than pediatric and cardiovascular radiologists. Conclusions: AI was generally viewed positively by radiologists, although notable concerns regarding data security, diagnostic trust, and job opportunities were also identified. AI was perceived as having the potential to improve workflow and reduce workload. Although AI may change the roles of radiologists, it is not expected to replace them entirely. Instead, it is likely to shift their responsibilities while helping reduce their workload. These findings are consistent with previous research and highlight AI’s potential to support healthcare professionals in delivering faster, more accurate, and more effective diagnostic services.

items.title: PERSONALITY AND ITS EMOTIONAL WILLPOWER
items.abstract: The article analyzes the relationship between personality and emotional willpower from a scientific and psychological perspective. Emotional willpower is interpreted as an individual’s ability to recognize and regulate emotional states, suppress impulsive tendencies, and overcome difficulties in achieving long-term goals. Drawing on classical (Vygotsky, Leontiev) and contemporary approaches (emotional intelligence, self-determination theory, and the Big Five model), the article explores the cognitive, motivational, and neuropsychological mechanisms underlying emotional willpower. The structure of personality, intrinsic motivation, emotional regulation, and developmental patterns throughout ontogenesis are examined in an interconnected manner. Practical approaches to developing emotional willpower are presented, and its significance for personal integration, stress resilience, and social adaptation is substantiated.

items.title: Personalized Learning Through Artificial Intelligence in a Low-Resource African Secondary School: A Constructivist and Self-Determination Theory Perspective from Burundi
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is widely credited with enabling personalized learning, yet evidence on how AI-driven personalization functions in low-resource, multilingual African classrooms remains scarce. This study examined how the integration of AI affects personalized learning outcomes at Discovery School, a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi. A convergent mixed-methods design combined a structured survey (n = 110: administrators, teachers, students, parents) with semi-structured interviews (n = 35), analyzed respectively in SPSS 27 (descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression) and NVivo 14 (six-phase thematic analysis, Cohen's κ = 0.83), and triangulated using a joint-display approach. The analysis was guided by Constructivist Learning Theory (CLT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Stakeholders reported high perceived AI effectiveness for personalized learning (M = 3.98, SD = 0.71), and students strongly valued the ability to learn at their own pace (M = 4.34, SD = 0.58; 89% agreement). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and student engagement were strongly and significantly correlated (r = 0.74-0.82, p < .01). Multiple regression showed that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, motivation, and infrastructure reliability jointly explained 46% of the variance in self-reported academic improvement (R² = 0.46), with perceived usefulness the strongest individual predictor (β = 0.42, p < .001). However, gains in engagement were not matched by corresponding gains in standardized test performance, revealing a perception-performance gap. Qualitative data showed teachers using AI dashboards diagnostically to scaffold instruction within students’ zones of proximal development, and students describing genuine, if algorithmically bounded, autonomy over pace and repetition. The study proposes two theoretical extensions — data-mediated constructivism and bounded autonomy — and concludes that AI functions as a pedagogical enhancer whose benefits are real but conditional on teacher capacity, infrastructure reliability, and equitable access, since 12.7% of respondents reported no reliable technology access outside school.

items.title: Pre-service EFL teachers’ conceptualizations of AI-supported adaptations to skill-based coursebook activities: a SAMR-based qualitative evaluation
items.abstract: Despite the growing interest in integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language teaching, limited research has examined the opportunities AI could provide for activity adaptations in English coursebooks. Through an exploratory qualitative design, this study aimed to reveal AI-supported adaptation suggestions from 25 pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers. It asked two questions: what activity adaptations for language skills are suggested and at which level the suggested adaptations in the Substitution-Augmentation-Modification-Redefinition (SAMR) framework are. The participants adapted one skill activity using AI and explained and justified their adaptations in written reports. The inductive thematic analysis of the reports revealed 19 adaptation suggestions, ten of which were in the transformation category and nine could serve as enhancements for traditional education practices according to the SAMR framework. Speaking was the skill with the highest number of suggested adaptations, followed by reading, writing, and listening skills. The common adaptation patterns among skills were AI as background knowledge supporter, AI as multicultural awareness builder, multimodal artefacts generator, and AI as a chatbot for oral and written practice. The study may contribute to discussions on AI supported materials development in EFL and teacher education fields by illustrating pre-service teachers’ conceptualizations of AI-supported coursebook activity adaptations and a critical evaluation of the suggestions through the SAMR.

items.title: Pre-service Teachers’ AI Usage: The Role of Perceived Usefulness, Subjective Norm, Behavioral Intention, and Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence in teacher education is seen as having great potential. AI tools can help alleviate teachers’ workloads and support learners individually. However, they are still relatively rarely used by practicing teachers and currently, there is a lack of empirical findings regarding the use of AI tools and the factors influencing AI usage behavior among pre-service teachers. Following Taylor and Todd (1995) by extending the Theory of Planned Behavior with the Technology Acceptance Model, this study investigates factors that influence pre-service teachers’ weekly use of AI. In an empirical-quantitative study, N = 931 pre-service teachers across Germany were asked about their perceived usefulness, subjective norm, self-efficacy beliefs, and behavioral intention to use AI tools in their future teaching practice. They also provided information about their average weekly AI usage time. The results of a structural equation model indicate that the behavioral intention to use AI tools in the future is significantly associated with perceived usefulness, subjective norm, and participants’ self-efficacy beliefs. Additionally, behavioral intention and self-efficacy beliefs are significantly linked with the weekly duration of AI use. Specifically, the association between pre-service teachers‘ self-efficacy beliefs and weekly AI use was partly accounted for statistically by behavioral intention. The results provide important insights into how to promote the use of AI tools in teacher education.

items.title: Predictive uncertainty representations in clinical AI shape physicians’ advice uptake, accuracy, and trust
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Machine-learning-based clinical decision support is entering routine care, but its value depends on whether clinicians can judge when to follow its advice and when to override it. Evidence suggests this judgment is often poorly calibrated in both directions. Whether displaying a model's predictive uncertainty helps physicians integrate advice more selectively is unclear. METHODS: In a preregistered, randomized vignette experiment, 227 physicians produced 1,802 sepsis risk assessments. Physicians gave an initial risk estimate, saw advice from a machine-learning system, and revised their estimate. They were randomized to see a risk score alone, or the score together with one of two visual representations of predictive uncertainty: icon arrays with uncertainty bands, or quantile dotplots. Outcomes were advice uptake, accuracy of the revised risk estimate, and trust. RESULTS: Here we show that both uncertainty representations increase advice uptake relative to the risk score alone, by 23% and 21%, and that the gap between correct and incorrect advice is descriptively about twice as large. Uptake of incorrect advice is not reliably reduced. Both formats improve the accuracy of revised risk estimates, with the larger effect for quantile dotplots, but only icon arrays increase trust. Physicians describe uncertainty as actionable only where they can tell why it is elevated. CONCLUSIONS: Displaying predictive uncertainty changes how physicians integrate machine-learning advice, but the representation format determines whether the benefit appears mainly as accuracy or trust. The effect is partial: uncertainty representations support recognizing reliable advice more than rejecting unreliable advice.

items.title: Predictors of AI Chatbot Use for Mental Health Support: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE To systematically review and quantitatively synthesize the evidence on the predictors of the use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health support. METHOD We searched PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, for quantitative studies that examined factors associated with the use of AI chatbots for mental health support. We assessed the methodological quality of the studies with the revised Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool for analytical cross-sectional studies. We pooled adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with random-effects models for predictors that had been examined in at least three studies, and we performed several sensitivity analyses. RESULTS We included eight cross-sectional studies with 7864 participants from the United States, Greece and Canada. items.title: Prevalencia y factores asociados al síndrome de burnout en el personal de enfermería de instituciones hospitalarias: Búsqueda narrativa
items.abstract: Introduction: Burnout syndrome represented a relevant occupational health problem among nursing staff due to constant exposure to physical, emotional, and organizational demands. The objective was to analyze its prevalence in hospital institutions and identify the main occupational, personal, and organizational factors associated with its occurrence. Methodology: A narrative search of scientific literature was conducted in biomedical and nursing databases, emphasizing recent publications and systematic reviews addressing prevalence, associated factors, and consequences of burnout. The evidence reviewed showed variations in prevalence estimates according to populations, hospital services, measurement instruments, and work contexts. A review published in 2025 identified global prevalence rates of 33.45% for emotional exhaustion, 25.0% for depersonalization, and 33.49% for low personal accomplishment. Results: The main associated factors were work overload, long working hours, shift work, time pressure, lack of organizational support, role conflicts, and occupational stress. Greater vulnerability was identified in high-demand areas, such as emergency departments and intensive care units. Burnout was also associated with physical and mental health problems, absenteeism, staff turnover, and reduced quality and safety of patient care. Conclusions: Burnout syndrome constituted a multifactorial problem that affected nursing staff well-being and the quality of hospital services. Prevention and early detection, together with improvements in working conditions, shift organization, communication, and institutional support, were considered essential to reducing associated factors and promoting safe patient care.

items.title: Prompting Depth as a Behavioural Proxy for Cognitive Engagement: A Learning Analytics Study of Student–Chatbot Dialogues in EFL Writing
items.abstract: Cognitive engagement shapes learning but resists direct observation, and the spread of generative-AI chatbots in EFL writing has made post hoc self-reports even harder to trust. This study asks whether the depth of a learner’s prompts (their specificity, elaboration, metacognitive framing, higher-order quality, and iterative refinement) can serve as a behavioural trace of that engagement. Using the RECIPE4U dataset (1,913 prompts from 130 EFL learners), two coders scored three prompt-level dimensions with substantial to near-perfect agreement (κ = .74–.84); the remaining dimensions were derived from intent annotations and session structure. The five dimensions did not behave as one construct. At the student level, only elaboration correlated with essay revision (r = .34) and, weakly, with satisfaction (r = .20); metacognitive framing and higher-order request added little, and iterative refinement related negatively to revision (r = −.18). An equal-weight composite showed no association with either criterion (r = .07). Each one-point increase in prompting depth was associated with more than twice the odds of subsequent revision (OR = 2.37; course-adjusted OR = 2.09), an association that persisted in a random-intercept model despite marked between-student variance (ICC = .41). Prompting depth is best read dimension by dimension: elaboration, not depth in the aggregate, tracks revision-oriented engagement.

items.title: Psychometric Evaluation of Situation Awareness and Workload Measures in a Nuclear Microworld Simulation
items.abstract: The increasing automation of nuclear power plants introduces novel demands on operator situation awareness and workload management. Yet, commonly used measures of situation awareness and workload often lack comprehensive validation within nuclear contexts. This study evaluates four prominent measures: two of situation awareness (3D SART and SACRI) and two of workload (NASA-TLX and a secondary task performance metric) according to key psychometric criteria for nuclear control room simulations. Using the Rancor Microworld platform, twenty-six participants completed both routine and abnormal scenarios under different automation levels, following a within-subjects design. SACRI correlated with generated revenue and task time, NASA-TLX correlated with temperature management and number of actions, and secondary task performance correlated with task time; 3D SART showed no correlations. Predictive analyses showed that these relationships largely disappeared when automation level and scenario type were included as covariates. Sensitivity to experimental conditions varied across measures, with 3D SART and NASA-TLX affected by automation level, and NASA-TLX, SACRI and secondary task performance by scenario type. Measures were not redundant, and all demonstrated moderate reliability across experimental conditions. Findings provide insight to researchers and nuclear practitioners for selecting situation awareness and workload assessment tools and strengthening the technical basis for designing safer and more effective control room systems.

items.title: QUALIDADE DE VIDA E ESTRESSE OCUPACIONAL EM AGENTES COMUNITÁRIOS DE SAÚDE NA ATENÇÃO PRIMÁRIA À SAÚDE
items.abstract: O estresse ocupacional e a qualidade de vida no trabalho constituem aspectos relevantes para a saúde dos Agentes Comunitários de Saúde (ACS) e para a organização da Atenção Primária à Saúde. Este estudo observacional, de abordagem quantitativa e delineamento transversal, descritivo e correlacional, teve como objetivo analisar esses constructos entre ACS do município de Santa Luzia, Paraíba, e investigar a associação entre eles. A pesquisa contou com 35 participantes, que responderam a um questionário sociodemográfico e profissional, a um instrumento de qualidade de vida no trabalho fundamentado no modelo de Walton e à Escala de Estresse no Trabalho. Os dados foram analisados por meio de estatística descritiva e correlação de Spearman. Os resultados evidenciaram nível elevado de estresse ocupacional e avaliação desfavorável da qualidade de vida no trabalho, com médias de 3,84 e 2,38, respectivamente. Identificou-se associação negativa e estatisticamente significativa entre os constructos, especialmente nas dimensões condições de trabalho e trabalho e espaço total de vida. Conclui-se que melhores condições laborais e maior equilíbrio entre trabalho e vida pessoal são aspectos importantes para a qualidade de vida dos ACS, destacando-se a necessidade de ações institucionais voltadas à valorização profissional, ao suporte organizacional e à promoção de ambientes de trabalho saudáveis.

items.title: Recursive Adversarial Engine: A Closed-Loop Cognitive Safety Framework for Autonomous AGI Evolution
items.abstract: Large language models are approaching general-purpose capability, yet three failure modes—hallucination, ethical misalignment, and cognitive rigidity—continue to block reliable deployment, and existing defenses address them only reactively at the output level. This paper presents the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a cognitive-safety infrastructure that treats contradiction as a source of negative entropy and organizes defense as a five-stage closed loop: definition, adversarial engagement, iterative verification, convergence, and ethical fusing. RAE formulates model self-correction as a recursive fixed-point problem, quantifies cognitive quality through topological metrics, distributes adversarial pressure across a pool of heterogeneous agents, and enforces ethical boundaries through dual-layer circuit breakers. A system specification and internal deployment observations indicate that the design targets self-referential vulnerability false-alarm rates below 1%, consensus variance at or above ln(2), and parallel adversarial pools exceeding 100 agents. We compare RAE with conventional filtering, instruction tuning, and static red teaming, and discuss the framework's theoretical status, evaluation limitations, and deployment requirements for high-stakes domains.

items.title: Researcherly Dispositions and Teachers’ Artificial Intelligence TPACK Development: A Two-Wave Repeated Cross-Sectional Study of Adult Intellectual Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming classroom teaching, yet two-wave repeated cross-sectional evidence on how K-12 teachers develop the knowledge that underpins intelligent performance with AI remains scarce. Our two-year study across 29 schools thus explored the associations between university-facilitated teacher action research and the development of artificial intelligence technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK), a domain-specific form of intelligence-as-knowledge in teaching. Data were collected using questionnaires on research-related dispositions and AI-TPACK with 285 participants in Year 1 and 200 participants in Year 2. Structural equation modeling suggested that the associations of teachers’ research consumption and production with their AI-TPACK differed between the two waves, possibly reflecting shifting program task requirements, whereas research attitude served as a stable predictor. The findings yield preliminary evidence regarding linkages between action research and teachers’ AI-TPACK, and highlight the differences in these associations across the two waves. Considered from the perspective of adult intellectual development, these results suggest that knowledge in professional practice might be sustained by opportunities to convert inquiry into produced knowledge, refining accounts of how expertise with intelligent technologies develops.

items.title: Same rules, mixed messages: exploring community perceptions of academic dishonesty in computing education
items.abstract: Academic dishonesty has long been a concern in computing education, and the rapid growth of online learning and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has further complicated how cheating is perceived and addressed. We report on a study examining how different actors in the computer science (CS) classroom interpret potential cheating scenarios and the motivations behind academic dishonesty. Participants included instructors (n = 6), teaching assistants (TAs; n = 22), and undergraduate students (n = 538) enrolled in two CS courses at a large Southeastern institution in the United States. Respondents classified scenarios as serious cheating, trivial cheating, or not cheating and responded to an open-ended question about motivations for academic dishonesty. Our findings reveal differences in perceptions across the three stakeholder groups. Among the instructors who participated, grade pressure and laziness were the most frequently mentioned motivations for academic dishonesty, whereas students and TAs more frequently emphasized gaps in prerequisite knowledge and time management challenges. Given the small instructor sample, these qualitative findings should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than representative of instructors more broadly. These results highlight differences in how academic dishonesty is understood across classroom stakeholders and underscore the need for clearer communication of academic-integrity expectations and instructional strategies that help students interpret and navigate those expectations in computing education, particularly in post-COVID learning environments where hybrid instruction, increased reliance on digital resources, and AI-assisted tools have reshaped students’ approaches to coursework and learning.

items.title: Shared control/autonomy in human-robot interaction: Current trends and the role of generative AI
items.abstract: In shared control and shared autonomy (SC/SA) systems, humans collaborate with robot agents to achieve common goals. Such systems enable collaborations beyond what either agent could do alone, benefiting from the relative strengths of humans (e.g., reasoning, planning) and robots (e.g., precision, repeatability). Research in this area dates back over 40 years, with numerous applications, such as in manufacturing, robot-assisted surgery, and assistive technologies. Shared control approaches have even seen some large-scale commercialization efforts in areas like semi-autonomous driving and automotive assembly. Without SC/SA, we may not have seen robots deployed in settings where manual teleoperation alone is too difficult, such as delicate laparoscopic surgical procedures or the remote operation of space manipulators. Recently, SC/SA approaches have gained significant traction, with hundreds of new methods published in scientific papers each year. In this paper, we examine recent approaches and trends in these methods, investigating several crucial aspects that are underexplored in previous surveys. We reviewed 195 papers across a 5-year time window (2020 to 2024) in three high-impact robotics venues (IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, and Science Robotics). First, we provide descriptive statistics and trends related to human input methods, technical approaches, and applications. Second, we provide a perspective on the growing role of generative artificial intelligence approaches in SC/SA. Based on these insights, we offer updated recommendations for future approaches.

items.title: Silent on Code? A Computing Lens on Generative AI Guidance at Canadian Polytechnics and Research Universities
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools now write, explain, and debug code, which changes how computing students learn and how their work is assessed. Instructors, however, act within institutional guidance written largely with essays in mind. We report a document analysis of the public, institution-level GenAI guidance of the 13 members of Polytechnics Canada and the 15 members of the U15 Group of Canadian Research Universities, retrieved in October 2026. Using a 27-item codebook spanning governance, integrity and assessment, data and legal issues, values, AI literacy, and a computing lens, we find that both sectors leave course-level decisions to instructors, although polytechnics more often prohibit use unless the instructor permits it (8 of 13 vs. 4 of 14), and converge on disclosure, links to academic integrity policy, and, in most institutions, the expectation that programs adapt rules to their discipline. Polytechnics frame GenAI as workforce preparation substantively far more often (7 of 13 vs. 0 of 14), whereas universities more often address assessment redesign. Twelve of 27 institutions with retrievable guidance mention code, but almost always as one output type among many; none names an AI coding assistant or provides substantive code-specific guidance on attribution, assessment, or licensing. Institution-level guidance is thus not silent on code but leaves programming-specific questions largely to programs and instructors. We propose five elements of discipline-level guidance for computing and release our codebook and coded dataset.

items.title: Situating AI Ethics in Language Education: Toward Justice, Relationality, and Pedagogy
items.abstract: Existing discussions of ethical AI often move between normative principles and localized accounts of ethical practice. We argue that these two orientations should not be treated as separate or competing. Normative values such as fairness, autonomy, and accountability must be examined in relation to how specific sociotechnical arrangements reproduce or intensify concrete injustices for differently positioned language users. Drawing on complementary scholarship in applied linguistics and philosophy, this article analyzes two sites of ethical tension: AI assessment systems and AI‐assisted language learning. In AI assessment, we show how fairness must account for how AI impacts assessment constructs and whether assessment judgments are answerable to learners. In AI‐assisted learning, we show how datafied personalization and algorithmic preemption reshape learner autonomy and language learning processes. Building on these analyses, we propose three directions for ethical AI in applied linguistics: moving toward the justice of AI‐mediated language practices, toward a relational understanding of learner autonomy, and toward AI ethics as pedagogy. We contend that ethical AI requires an ongoing responsibility to preserve language users’ space to negotiate AI in ways that expand rather than narrow their multilingual meaning‐making resources and communicative possibilities.

items.title: SmartLens: Turning AI Agent Changes into Learning, Review, and Risk Signals in the IDE
items.abstract: Developers increasingly act as managers of AI agents: they hand tasks to AI coding agents and then have to understand, verify, ship, and learn from what the agents produce. IDEs and recent tools can show which committed lines were written by AI, but they do not attribute the pending changes of external agents, and they do not use attribution to help the developer review, learn, or judge risk. We present SmartLens, an IntelliJ IDEA plugin that attributes changes to an AI agent, the developer, or both. It combines this attribution with the Git history to support three goals: (i) Learn compares the skills (APIs, language features, annotations) that agents used with the skills the developer has used in their own commits; (ii) Understand ranks pending changes by review priority; and (iii) Risk shows hotspots: files that change often, are mostly written by AI, and that the developer barely knows. In a preliminary evaluation, SmartLens attributed 8 of 12 scripted IDE scenarios correctly; all failures were in (expected) blind spots. On 8 Open Source Software repositories with agent co-authored commits, agents introduced up to 253 skills that do not appear in the main developer's own commits. The Risk ranking was as good as or better than plain churn at predicting later bug fixes, but part of this gain is due to recency.

items.title: Social Influence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Preference for Humans Does Not Deter Artificial Intelligence Influence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a source of social influence. But people often prefer human over AI sources (algorithm aversion/preference for humans), which might prevent AI from influencing humans. However, we outline a theoretical framework that suggests that preferences do not play a causal role in influence. To test this framework, we investigated under which conditions preferences predict AI influence. Participants (N = 1,254) indicated their adviser preference and then made incentivised decisions while receiving advice from AI or human advisers. Participants preferred human over AI advisers but were influenced by AI and humans similarly. A strong aversion to AI advisers had no (Study 1) or a trivial relation (Study 2 and 3) with AI influence, which was explained by confounding variables. When manipulated, preferences did not predict advice-taking, but adviser trustworthiness and competence did (Study 3). Our results suggest that for predicting AI influence, understanding domain-specific social cognitions, not preferences, is critical.

items.title: Spanning boundaries in socio-technological transformation: practical approaches for developing and iterating shared mental models
items.abstract: This article in the journal Gruppe. Interaktion. Organisation. (GIO) examines how organizations can intentionally develop, maintain, and continuously adapt shared mental models (SMMs) across team, functional, and hierarchical boundaries. Whereas prior research has primarily investigated the characteristics, measurement, and effects of SMMs within teams, comparatively less is known about how shared cognitive orientations emerge and can be cultivated within heterogeneous organizational and socio-technological networks. This question is particularly relevant to socio-technological transformation and human-AI collaboration, where divergent professional perspectives, technological systems, and evolving task allocations intensify the need for cognitive alignment. Based on a structured narrative literature review, the paper conceptualizes SMMs as boundary spanning cognitive infrastructures and derives overarching enabling conditions and five principles for their development and maintenance. Leadership, organizational culture, and psychological safety provide the necessary enabling conditions. Joint situational analysis, visual and scenario-based co-construction, and interdisciplinary skill profiles and shared language support SMM development. Iterative feedback loops and the deliberate unlearning of outdated assumptions enable their continuous adaptation. Actor-Network Theory complements this perspective by explaining how shared understandings emerge through translation, are mediated by material and digital artefacts, and become stabilized within socio-technical networks. The paper thereby extends SMM research toward an organization-wide and process-oriented perspective and provides actionable guidance for managing socio-technological transformation.

items.title: Strategi Inovasi Pendidikan Berkelanjutan Berbasis Kecerdasan Buatan dan Transformasi Digital dalam Membangun Kompetensi Generasi Muda Berwawasan Lingkungan
items.abstract: Perkembangan kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan transformasi digital telah membawa perubahan dalam penyelenggaraan pendidikan serta membuka peluang untuk menciptakan pembelajaran yang lebih adaptif dan inovatif. Namun, pemanfaatan teknologi dalam pendidikan perlu diintegrasikan dengan prinsip pembangunan berkelanjutan agar mampu mendukung pengembangan kompetensi generasi muda yang memiliki kepedulian terhadap lingkungan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis strategi inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan berbasis kecerdasan buatan dan transformasi digital dalam membangun kompetensi generasi muda berwawasan lingkungan. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dengan pendekatan deskriptif kualitatif. Pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui penelusuran, pemilihan, dan pengkajian artikel jurnal ilmiah yang relevan, kemudian dianalisis melalui tahapan identifikasi, pengelompokan, perbandingan, dan sintesis temuan berdasarkan fokus penelitian. Hasil kajian menunjukkan enam aspek utama dalam inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan, yaitu transformasi digital sebagai fondasi pembelajaran adaptif, pemanfaatan AI untuk mendukung personalisasi dan efisiensi pembelajaran, penguatan kompetensi pendidik, integrasi Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), penerapan pembelajaran kontekstual berbasis Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) dan Project-Based Learning (PjBL), serta pengembangan kompetensi generasi muda. Hasil kajian juga menunjukkan bahwa penggunaan AI secara berlebihan berpotensi mengurangi keterlibatan peserta didik dalam proses berpikir sehingga diperlukan penguatan literasi digital dan kemampuan berpikir kritis. Dengan demikian, inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan perlu mengintegrasikan teknologi, kompetensi pendidik, dan pendekatan pembelajaran yang berorientasi pada keberlanjutan untuk mendukung terbentuknya generasi muda yang kritis, kreatif, adaptif, serta memiliki literasi dan kepedulian lingkungan.

items.title: Structural Intelligence: Consolidated Research Corpus and Source Archive (2026)
items.abstract: This repository presents the consolidated research corpus of Structural Intelligence (SI), an interdisciplinary theoretical framework developed by Vladisav Jovanović within the broader research program of the Philosophy of Structure. The collection reorganizes 27 original publications into seven integrated manuscripts: Coherence, Contact, and Answerability; The Architecture of Correction; Evidence-Constrained Interpretation; Structural Debt; Structural Capture; Organization and Adaptation; and Wisdom Under Pressure. Together, these manuscripts examine the relationships between coherence, evidence, warranted correction, adaptive organization, human agency, and the distribution of unresolved costs. They situate the framework in relation to established research in epistemology, cognitive psychology, cybernetics, systems theory, enactivism, organizational learning, resilience engineering, and artificial intelligence evaluation. Structural Intelligence is presented as an integrative conceptual framework with testable research hypotheses, rather than a universal causal theory or a validated psychometric construct. The repository preserves the original manuscripts, revised consolidated publications, source inventories, content-preservation documentation, and SHA-256 checksums. Editable manuscript sources and supporting materials are included where available. Its purpose is to reduce bibliographic fragmentation while preserving the intellectual development, provenance, and conceptual contributions of the original research. The collection provides a coherent foundation for subsequent theoretical development, independent evaluation, and empirical investigation.

items.title: Supporting Without Taking Over: AI Support in Gratitude Writing
items.abstract: Gratitude writing can support well-being, but independent practice may lack guidance. Generative AI could help while shaping reflection, agency, and ownership. We investigated how gratitude-writing format and AI-assistance mode influence well-being and writing experiences. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (N=401), participants completed a gratitude reflection or a gratitude letter using two AI-assistance modes: scaffolding, which provided reflective questions after inactivity, or co-writing, which offered inline text suggestions. Participants' well-being improved after using our AI-assisted gratitude-writing system, consistent with the activity's intended benefits. However, participants' experiences revealed a trade-off between the AI-support types: co-writing received higher usability ratings, yet its immediacy could disrupt writing, and greater suggestion acceptance was associated with weaker perceived agency. Scaffolding supported stronger perceived human ownership but was sometimes overlooked. These findings extend human-AI writing research beyond productivity and text quality by showing how AI involvement shapes psychological outcomes and the experience of self-guided, emotionally meaningful writing.

items.title: The Association of Behavioral Intention to Use Artificial Intelligence with Entrepreneurial Alertness and Intention Among University Students
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased interest in understanding individuals’ intention to use AI. However, little is known about how this intention is related to entrepreneurial alertness (EA) and entrepreneurial intention (EI). This study examined the relationships among behavioral intention to use AI (BI-AI), EA, and EI among university students in Türkiye. It also explored whether trait competitiveness (TC) and family entrepreneurial background (FB) moderate the relationship between EA and EI. Data were collected from 355 participants through an online cross-sectional survey. The measurement model was evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis together with reliability and validity assessments. PROCESS macro analyses with bootstrap confidence intervals were then used to test the proposed direct, indirect, and moderating relationships. The results showed that BI-AI was positively related to EA (b = 0.111, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [0.054, 0.167]). However, no significant direct relationship was found between BI-AI and EI (b = −0.017, SE = 0.078, 95% CI [−0.170, 0.135]. EA was positively related to EI (b = 1.136, SE = 0.142, 95% CI [0.857, 1.414]). The indirect relationship between BI-AI and EI through EA was also significant (b = 0.126, SE = 0.060, 95% CI [0.026, 0.256]). In the moderation analysis (N = 351), trait competitiveness significantly moderated the relationship between EA and EI (b = 0.231, SE = 0.060, 95% CI [0.113, 0.348]). Family entrepreneurial background, however, did not significantly moderate this relationship (b = −0.203, SE = 0.140, 95% CI [−0.478, 0.073]). The data indicate that EA may be relevant to understanding the link between BI-AI and EI and that the association between EA and EI is stronger among those with higher levels of TC. Because the study relied on cross-sectional data, the results should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than proof that one condition causes another. Future longitudinal and intervention-based research may provide a better understanding of how BI-AI, EA, and EI evolve over time.

items.title: The Cognitive Dimension of Complexity: On the Limits of Formalization and the Development of Cognitive Capabilities in the Age of AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) automates work for which established methods of problem formulation and solution already exist, the ability to act where such methods do not yet exist or no longer apply becomes relatively more valuable. This paper examines a cognitive dimension of complexity arising from the relationship between the properties of the reality under investigation and the cognitive capabilities of the subject (an individual or a team). Even before a problem is explicitly formulated, the language used to describe a real situation can introduce distortions. Three types of difficulty are distinguished by what must change: the model, the problem space, or the cognitive capabilities of the subject. AI can reinforce existing limitations as well as help reveal them; the outcome depends on how human–AI interaction is organized. The paper outlines a research agenda for Complexity Lab in which interaction with reality under incomplete knowledge may itself become a mechanism of cognitive development. It is addressed to leaders in business, engineering, and applied science.

items.title: The cost of being seen as AI in group bargaining
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in collective decision-making, people's perceptions of AI may shape who reaches agreement and what they receive. We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.

items.title: THE DIDACTIC GAME IN CONTEMPORARY TEACHING – ANALYSES AND CHALLENGE
items.abstract: Play represents an important factor in the learning process and the development of children's personalities, particularly when it is purposefully used as a means of achieving educational objectives. Contemporary educational approaches increasingly emphasize teaching practices that encourage students' active participation, intrinsic motivation, creativity and independent learning. In this context, the concept of “Learning through Play” represents an important foundation for reconsidering traditional teaching practices and the possibilities of integrating play into contemporary education. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the pedagogical significance of didactic games, with particular reference to the UNESCO report “Why the World Needs Happy Schools: Global Report on Happiness in and for Learning” (2024). The aim is to examine the relationship between learning through play, active student participation, motivation and the creation of a supportive learning environment. The paper applies a qualitative theoretical and analytical approach based on content analysis of the document and interpretation of relevant scientific research. Particular attention is given to the teacher's role in planning and guiding play-based activities, as well as to the conditions under which didactic games can contribute to meaningful and quality learning. The paper concludes that didactic games should not be understood merely as additional or entertaining activities, but as a pedagogically designed approach that connects knowledge with experience, activity and students' personal engagement.

items.title: The Influence of Artificial Intelligence Chatbots on Customer Experience, Satisfaction and Brand Loyalty in E-Commerce
items.abstract: AI chatbots are making their way into ecommerce as "24/7" on-demand interfaces to guide, resolve, and inquiry. However, its implementation does not promise a better experience or increased brand attachment. We theorize from available research about chatbot property-construals on consumers' experience and satisfaction, and how those experiences lead to retention, repurchase and loyalty. A structured integrative review of peer reviewed empirical articles and reviews, derived mainly from 2020 to November 2026, and the extant literature on customer experience, information-systems success and expectation-confirmation was conducted in which publications were analyzed via thematic comparisons and a study-level matrix; no primary data, pooled effects, or statistical models were studied. Consistently, responsiveness, informational quality, relevance, reliability and service recovery lead to positive end-states; empathy and social presence foster trust, and social cues (such as humanlike appearance) may do so as well. Meta-analyses show that chatbot satisfaction is positively correlated with behavioral intentions but that the relatively large between-studies heterogeneity tempers the generality of these findings. Research in other industries shows that although chatbots can grab consumers' attention, its effects on emotional stimulation are uncertain and technology-induced errors cause cognitive dissonance, with accompanying frustration and reduced service quality ratings. We conclude with an integrative journey framework involving interaction personality-construals, experience, satisfaction and outcomes. Chatbots will be most effective at engendering loyalty if they guide consumers accurately, effectively and with good timing, manage their own capabilities and provide quick escalation procedures when conditions demand.

items.abstract: This exploratory study illuminates the “black box” of student reasoning by examining how information systems students engaged with generative AI tools (ChatGPT) during a complex SQL exam. Using qualitative thematic analysis of 33 interaction transcripts, we identified preliminary behavioral patterns that differentiate successful from unsuccessful problem-solving. In this sense, these interactions resemble a digital think-aloud, in which AI transcripts provide insights into the internal thought processes associated with problem-solving. Analysis suggests a spectrum of interactions from “Strategic AI Engagement” (the “pilot”) to “Procedural AI Dependency” (the “passenger”). Successful engagements appeared to involve iterative refinement, systematic validation, and adaptive strategy shifts. Conversely, unsuccessful interactions tended to reflect a conceptual bypass characterized by passive query reception, rigid approaches, and an abdication of technical reasoning to the AI. The findings suggest that as technical proficiency shifts from procedural code generation toward evaluative judgment, educators should design AI-assisted assignments that prioritize auditing, verification, and strategic questioning. More broadly, the study suggests that GenAI can support but not replace the foundational competence and reflective judgment essential for effective problem-solving in data-driven professional environments.

items.title: The Price of Progress
items.abstract: This multidisciplinary perspective paper examines the rise of artificial intelligence, robotics and automation and their potential effects on human employment and livelihood. The paper considers technological progress from economic, psychological, social, philosophical, ethical and religious perspectives. It explores how automation may transform employment in hospitality, manufacturing, transportation, retail, administrative work and other sectors while also considering the new forms of employment that technological development may create. Particular attention is given to the human consequences of involuntary job displacement, including financial insecurity, identity, dignity, psychological wellbeing and economic inequality. The paper also examines the responsibilities of technology developers, employers, governments, workers and consumers during periods of technological transition. A distinctive part of the discussion considers Islamic concepts of justice, Rizq, human responsibility and the supplication of the oppressed in relation to technological displacement. This religious discussion is presented as ethical analysis and does not constitute a formal Islamic legal ruling or fatwa. The paper ultimately argues for human centred automation, in which technological progress is evaluated not only by efficiency and productivity but also by its contribution to human dignity, security and wellbeing. This is a perspective paper based on secondary research and personal interpretation. It does not present original experimental or survey data.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important component of modern education, particularly in the field of English language teaching. The integration of AI-powered educational technologies creates new opportunities for improving language acquisition, developing communicative competence, and providing individualized learning experiences. This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, focusing on its potential to enhance the four fundamental language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. The study explores the pedagogical advantages of AI-based tools, including personalized instruction, automated feedback, adaptive learning, and increased learner motivation. Furthermore, it considers the challenges associated with AI integration, such as technological dependence, limited digital literacy, data privacy, and the importance of maintaining the teacher's professional role. The article emphasizes that artificial intelligence should be regarded as a supportive educational instrument rather than a replacement for human teachers. The effective implementation of AI requires a balanced approach that combines technological innovation with pedagogical principles and learner-centred instruction.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Multidisciplinary Tumor Boards for Breast Cancer: A Critical Review
items.abstract: Multidisciplinary tumor boards (MTBs) are the gold standard for breast cancer (BC) treatment planning, but rising caseloads and the growing number of clinical, pathological, and molecular factors under consideration are straining their capacity. AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), has been proposed as a decision support tool, and BC is the tumor type for which AI-MTB concordance has been studied most. We conducted a narrative critical review of studies comparing AI-generated treatment recommendations with breast MTB recommendations, along with evidence on MTB performance, earlier rule-based decision support systems, and the relevant regulatory and medico-legal environment. We evaluated 17 LLM studies published between 2023 and 2026. Overall concordance ranged from 16% to 94%, increasing with model generation, structured input, and guideline grounding, and decreasing with disease stage and case complexity. Concordance was consistently high for endocrine therapy and standard indications for systemic therapy, variable for surgery, radiotherapy, and genomic testing, and low or inconsistent for genetic counseling, anti-HER2 regimen selection, and the management of metastatic disease. Reproducibility was poor, and no study examined patient outcomes. Concordance with the MTB is not equivalent to clinical correctness, and hallucinations, the handling of incomplete information, and automation bias are distinct safety dimensions that concordance does not capture; we therefore propose a multidimensional evaluation framework. The current, limited evidence base supports using AI as a supervised, guideline-grounded pre-MTB tool in treatment planning rather than as a replacement for the MTB itself.

items.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
items.abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

items.title: The stock market hallucination paradox: explanation depth, conversational naturalness and epistemic trust in GenAI assistants
items.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how the explanation depth and conversational naturalness of generative AI (GenAI) stock assistants relate to retail investors' perceived epistemic trust, perceived control, continuance intention and self-reported value co-creation, and how hallucination risk, overload and literacy condition these associations. Design/methodology/approach – Drawing on cognitive appraisal and epistemic trust theories, a cross-sectional survey of 386 Indonesian retail investors was analyzed with PLS-SEM, Gaussian copulas, PLSpredict, CVPAT and importance–performance map analysis (IPMA). Findings – Both design features were positively associated with trust and control, which were associated with continuance and co-creation. Perceived hallucination risk strengthened the explanation depth–trust association but weakened the naturalness–trust association. Overload was negatively related to control without significantly moderating the design features. Literacy moderated the trust–outcome associations in opposite directions. The explanation depth–control path was not robust to endogeneity correction. Research limitations/implications – The cross-sectional, self-reported, single-country design precludes causal inference; trust calibration against actual AI accuracy was not assessed. Practical implications – Providers could prioritize verifiable, layered explanations over conversational polish; regulators could consider disclosure and verification-literacy guidance. Originality/value – The study introduces perceived stock data hallucination risk as a context-specific construct and links perceived trust and self-reported engagement to managerial priorities.

items.title: The times they are AI-changin: my personal experience with artificial intelligence
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: I chronicle a new, unique paradigm shift at the intersection of human creativity and generative artificial intelligence. Following my retirement, I engaged the large language model Google Gemini as a digital co-pilot for my administrative and scientific activities. CASE STUDY: What began as a tool for basic text formatting, rapidly evolved into a sophisticated, synergistic collaboration, culminating in the co-authorship of a quantitative scientific manuscript in the field of "cultural musicology", a totally new field of investigation for me. AI ADVANTAGES: Based on my experience, I explore the profound structural advantages of AI assistants over human counterparts, emphasizing twenty-four-hour availability, near-instantaneous manuscript synthesis, and rapid drafting capabilities. SYSTEMIC RISKS: I present a stark, cautionary analysis regarding the inevitable proliferation of autonomous, potentially malicious digital entities. I foresee an imminent epidemic of scientific paper retractions driven by unverified or intentionally corrupted data, raising the dystopian prospect of an algorithmic enforcement class or digital containment firewalls. CONCLUSIONS: AI is here to stay but it should be strictly regulated to avoid or minimize the undesirable serious consequences in science.

items.title: Theory of human–machine co-creation
items.abstract: Humans have long used machines to support creative work. Generative artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for human–machine co-creation, in which computational systems generate and refine propositions in interaction with humans. However, the mechanisms and operations underlying these interactions remain insufficiently understood. We therefore propose a theory of human–machine co-creation. Our premise is that the human and the machine each have a distinct concept space and a knowledge space of their own, and that co-creation proceeds through the assimilation and elaboration of concepts and knowledge from each other’s propositions within these spaces. The proposed theory defines the mechanisms of adoption, abortion, and adaptation in human–machine co-creation, explaining when, why, and how the collaborators, i.e., humans and machines, accept, reject, or transform each other’s propositions. It further articulates the operations through which new concepts and knowledge are generated. The theory offers an ontology and an epistemology for understanding how humans and machines collaborate, and provides a foundation for describing these interactions and predicting their creative outcome.

items.title: THINKING BEFORE PROMPTING: LINKING SPATIAL REASONING, CRITICAL THINKING AND GENERATIVE AI THROUGH THE SPARC FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) produced explanations, diagrams and worked solutions in seconds, which raised a pedagogical dilemma: better task completion did not show that learners had practised the reasoning needed for independent performance. This conceptual paper examined the intersection of spatial reasoning, scientific reasoning and critical thinking in AI-supported higher education. A focused, illustrative synthesis of research on spatial cognition, cognitive offloading, human-AI interaction and educational scaffolding identified a plausible mechanism of concern: when AI supplied both a representation and its interpretation, students could bypass the construction, transformation and checking of mental models. The paper distinguished supportive from substitutive offloading and proposed SPARC (Sketch, Predict, Audit, Reconstruct, Calibrate), a five-stage instructional sequence that preserved learner-generated spatial and causal reasoning while using AI as a fallible comparison partner. Two teaching vignettes from introductory physics, the vertical motion of a tossed ball and work and power in stair climbing, showed how the sequence could be implemented with brief written or visual artefacts and assessed with an illustrative rubric. Four falsifiable propositions and a feasible pilot design were formulated for classroom evaluation. SPARC was not presented as an empirically validated intervention, and the available studies did not establish that GenAI necessarily caused durable declines in critical thinking. The paper concluded that educational evaluation should examine unaided transfer, reasoning quality and confidence calibration, rather than the quality of AI-assisted products alone.
